summary.text: Abinadi was a Nephite prophet raised up by the Lord to reprove the wicked people of King Noah for their sins. He delivered prophecies warning that if the people did not repent, they would face bondage, famine, pestilence, and death. When they refused to repent, Abinadi reappeared in disguise and pronounced greater woes upon them. He was taken by the priests of the king, with whom he had a long controversy on the principle of the atonement and other laws of God. Condemned to death, he was burned at the stake in the City of Lehi-Nephi. Alma the elder pleaded for Abinadi’s life, and later made a record of his teachings, preserving some of the most precious gospel teachings in the Book of Mormon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Abish was a Lamanite woman who served as a servant-maid to the queen of King Lamoni. She had been converted to the Lord many years earlier through a vision granted to her father, though she never spoke of it. During Ammon's mission to the Lamanites, she witnessed Lamoni and his court, including Ammon, being overcome by the power of God. Understanding this divine power, she ran through the city to share what had happened, prompting a crowd to gather at the palace. When tensions arose, she returned and helped the queen and her husband rise from the ground, leading to the queen expressing gratitude to the Savior and her husband teaching the Gospel. Abish played a key role in the great conversion of the Lamanites and is mentioned only in connection with this event in the Book of Mormon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amlici was a Nephite who sought to overturn the republic and establish a monarchy in the days of the Judges. His ambition was to be king of the Nephites, but after the people rejected his pretensions, his followers consecrated him king. He raised an army and fought a battle near the hill Amnihu against Alma, the younger, resulting in heavy casualties on both sides. After his defeat, Amlici's followers joined invading Lamanites in the land Minon, where they were later defeated by Alma's troops. Amlici was slain in single combat by Alma, and his followers fled to Hermounts, where many died. Amlici belonged to the order of Nehor and was described as cunning and worldly-wise.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ammaron was the son of Amos the elder, a descendant of Alma and Nephi. He received sacred records from his brother Amos, the younger, and later hid them due to the moral decline of the Nephites. He concealed the records in the land Antum, in a hill called Shim, and informed Mormon, then a ten-year-old child, of their location. Ammaron instructed Mormon to retrieve the plates of Nephi and record observations about the people when he turned twenty-four, while leaving the rest of the records undisturbed. Ammaron’s father, Amos the elder, had died 126 years before Ammaron buried the sacred engravings, indicating Ammaron was likely very old at the time.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ammoron was a Nephite traitor and apostate, a descendant of Zoram and the brother of Amalickiah, whom he succeeded as ruler of the Lamanites in B.C. 66. He was slain by Teancum in the city of Moroni in B.C. 61 and succeeded by his son Tubaloth. After his brother's death, Ammoron left the land of Zarahemla, repaired to the land of Nephi, informed the widowed queen of her loss, and gathered a vast host of men to continue the war, especially on the western border. He determined to carry on hostilities with vigor but lacked his brother's military skill, allowing the Nephites to reclaim much of the territory lost to Amalickiah. Ammoron is notable for his correspondence with Moroni regarding an exchange of prisoners of war, which highlights his character.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amulek was a Nephite prophet and a man of wealth and importance who lived in the city of Ammonihah, situated near the land of Melek on the west side of the river Sidon. He met Alma, the younger, a prophet who had been cast out of the city, and helped nourish him. Together, they preached in Ammonihah, but faced persecution from the people, who grew more wicked and eventually martyred the saints. Amulek witnessed the martyrdom and was later imprisoned but was miraculously freed by divine power. He went to the land of Sidom, then to Zarahemla, where he continued preaching with Alma. Amulek also preached to the Zoramites and the people of Jershon, showing great faith and zeal for the gospel.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amulon was a prominent priest under King Noah who participated in the martyrdom of the Prophet Abinadi. After Noah's death, Amulon fled into the wilderness with other priests, eventually settling in the land of Amulon. There, he and his associates married Lamanite women, sparking a conflict between the Lamanites and Nephites. Later, Amulon was appointed ruler of the lands of Amulon and Helam, where he oppressed the people of God. He also taught the Lamanites the learning of the Nephites but omitted teachings about the Lord or the law of Moses. His role as a leader and educator significantly impacted the Lamanites, though his death remains unrecorded.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Anti-Nephi-Lehi was the son of the king of the Lamanites and a brother of Lamoni. He succeeded his father as ruler of the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, a group of Lamanites who had converted to Christianity. These people were later called Ammonites when they moved to the lands of the Nephites. Anti-Nephi-Lehi faced rebellion from unrepentant Lamanites, who massacred thousands of their original people. To avoid extinction, the Christians moved to Jershon. The Nephite apostates and their descendants later controlled Lamanite affairs. Anti-Nephi-Lehi was likely alive when the king was killed by Amalickiah's men, and his successors—Amalickiah, Ammoron, and Tubeloth—unquestionably had Nephite blood.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Corianton was the son of Alma and one of his brothers who participated in a mission to the Zoramites. He struggled with youthful arrogance and skepticism, doubting key doctrines and justifying his sins through self-serving reasoning. He abandoned his mission to be with Isabel, a harlot, which hindered the work of his fellow missionaries. Alma later chided him for his actions and explained the doctrines Corianton had questioned. Corianton later accompanied his father on missionary travels and, after Alma's death, worked under his brother Helaman. He survived his elder brothers and, at the time of Shiblon's death, was in North America delivering provisions to settlers, suggesting he had repented and proven himself worthy of responsibility.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Ether was the last great prophet of the Jaredites and the author of the Book of Ether, an abridgment of his writings made by Moroni. He predicted the destruction of his people and the survival of Coriantumr, the last Jaredite king, and foretold the coming of Christ, the New Jerusalem, and the last dispensation. Ether lived in hiding in a rock cavity, recording events as they unfolded, and witnessed the destruction of his people at Ramah (Cumorah). He hid the twenty-four golden plates containing his record, which were later found by the people of King Limhi. Ether's writings provide a detailed history of the Jaredites and the dealings of the Lord with humanity from his time to the end of time.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gadianton was a Nephite apostate who founded and led the robber bands that bore his name. He organized a band of followers bound by secret oaths and covenants, which he claimed were revealed to him by the same being that had whispered them to Cain. Gadianton was a cunning and strategic man who sought to be elected chief judge of the Nephite commonwealth, with his followers' support. He directed his band to attempt to kill Helaman, the Chief Judge, but the plot failed when Kishkumen, his lieutenant, was slain. The band then fled into the hills and wilderness, where they retreated whenever threatened. Gadianton's followers participated in secret meetings and consented to his ambitions, but no further details of his personal life are recorded.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Giddianhi was a leader of the Gadianton robbers who lived during the time of the Savior. He was a bold and capable leader who threatened the Nephites with destruction unless they surrendered to the robbers. He wrote to Lachoneus, the chief governor of the Nephites, but Lachoneus did not heed his warning. Instead, Lachoneus directed the Nephites to gather in the lands of Zarahemla and Bountiful. Giddianhi later led the robbers in a major battle against the Nephites, who had removed all food from their homes, leaving the robbers without sufficient supplies. In the battle, the Nephites were victorious, and Giddianhi was slain. He was succeeded by Zemnarihah as commander of the robbers.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gideon was a Nephite patriot born in the land of Lehi-Nephi who took a leading part in the rebellion against the iniquitous king Noah. He sought to kill Noah but later spared him, leading to Noah's flight and eventual death at the hands of his own people. Gideon played a key role in the deliverance of the people of Limhi and in ending hostilities during a war involving Lamanite maidens. He was a respected teacher in the Church, possibly holding a higher priesthood, and was slain by Nehor for opposing his teachings. A city was named after him in honor of his service and sacrifice.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gidgiddoni was a prophet-general of the Nephites during the time of Christ, serving as commander-in-chief of the armies of the commonwealth and sharing governmental powers with Lachoneus, the elder. He led the Nephites in gathering and fortifying their people in a region of refuge, directing the assembled hosts and supporting Lachoneus in this effort. Gidgiddoni played a key role in defending against the robbers, making successful sorties, intercepting their forces, and leading the soldiers in capturing and converting many of them. He also led the people in rebuilding their cities and improving their lands, and his leadership was instrumental in breaking up the bands of robbers and restoring peace and righteousness.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amalekites were a sect of Nephite apostates whose origin is not given. Many followed the order of Nehor and early on affiliated with the Lamanites, helping to build a city called Jerusalem near the waters of Mormon. Known for being crafty and hard-hearted, they resisted conversion efforts by the sons of Mosiah, with only one person converted. They led the massacres of the Christian Lamanites, or people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, and later, Lamanite generals often placed them in high command due to their strong character, intense hatred for former brethren, and violent tendencies. They are frequently associated with the Zoramites and Amulonites in the sacred record.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amalickiahites were followers of Amalickiah who sought to destroy the Church and replace the Nephite republic with a monarchy. After finding their numbers insufficient and facing doubts among their ranks, they traveled to the land of Nephi with the goal of joining the Lamanites. Moroni intercepted them in the wilderness, leading to Amalickiah's escape to the Lamanites while most of the Amalickiahites were captured and taken back to Zarahemla. They were then given the choice to make a covenant to support the cause of liberty or face death. Only a few refused the covenant.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amlicites were followers of Amlici who fled to Hermounts after their dispersion. They marked themselves with red on their foreheads, like the Lamanites, but did not shave their heads. They were not aware they were fulfilling a prophecy when they acted, as it was not their intention to follow the words of those they had seceded from.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Amulonites were descendants of Amulon and his associates, corrupt priests of King Noah. They were Nephites on their fathers' side and Lamanites on their mothers', but by association and education, they aligned with the Lamanites. Many later rejected their fathers' conduct and adopted the name Nephites. Those who remained Amulonites followed Nehor and were scattered in the lands of Amulon, Helam, and Jerusalem. They persecuted the people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, alongside the Amalekites, and later were killed in a battle led by Zoram. Survivors fled to the east wilderness, usurped power over the people of Laman, and caused many to be burned for believing in the Gospel. Lamanites eventually hunted and killed them, fulfilling Abinadi's prophecy that they would suffer death by fire, as he had.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Anti-Nephi-Lehies was a group of people better known as the Ammonites or the people of Ammon, named in honor of Ammon, the son of king Mosiah II, who played a leading role in converting them to the truth.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gadianton Robbers were a secretive and violent group that caused significant harm to the Nephites. Originating from ancient traditions linked to Cain, they flourished among the Antediluvians and Jaredites, and were responsible for the downfall of both the Jaredite and Nephite races. They aspired to rule the republic, murdered Nephite chief judges, and fought in wars with the Nephites and Lamanites, including during the earthly life of Jesus. Giddianhi, their leader, once wrote to Lachoneus, urging submission to their ways. Lachoneus later gathered Nephites and Lamanites to suppress the robbers, who were eventually destroyed by famine and conflict. After Jesus' time, the Gadianton Robbers spread across the land and contributed to the atrocities in the final wars between Nephites and Lamanites.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Jaredites were the descendants of Jared and his associates, led by the power of God from the Tower of Babel to this continent, where they became one of the mightiest nations and flourished in a manner unsurpassed in the history of the post-deluvian races. They eventually fell into decay through corruption and iniquity, were ultimately destroyed in a desolating internecine war, and only Coriantumr remained as their representative. Their destruction occurred around the same time the Nephites reached this land.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Lamanites were a people who, along with the Nephites, inhabited the American continent from about 590 B.C. to 385 A.D. They destroyed the Nephites and became the sole possessors of the land. The American Indians are considered their degraded descendants. The Lamanites originated from the half tribe of Manasseh and were named after Laman, the eldest son of Lehi. Originally, they were the children of Laman, Lemuel, and some of the family of Ishmael. Over time, they intermixed with the Nephites, and the names Lamanite and Nephite became more indicative of religion and civilization than of birth.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nephites were a people descended from Manasseh, the son of Joseph, and named after Nephi, the fourth son of Lehi. They occupied the American continent from around 590 B.C. to 385 A.D., when they were destroyed by the Lamanites. Originally descended from Nephi, Sam, Jacob, Joseph, and Zoram, the distinction between Nephites and Lamanites became more about religion and government than ancestry over time.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Zoramites were a family of the Nephites, descendants of Zoram, who received blessings with and were joined to the posterity of Nephi.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ishmael was a righteous Israelite from the tribe of Ephraim who lived in Jerusalem around 600 B.C. He had five marriageable daughters and several grown sons. The sons of Lehi invited Ishmael and his family to join them on their journey to a promised land. Though Ishmael was faithful to the Lord during the journey, some of his sons showed rebellious behavior. After arriving at Nahom, Ishmael died, causing sorrow and prompting further unrest among his family. His eldest daughter married Zoram, and four of his other daughters married the sons of Lehi.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

jared-jaredite-founder.name: Jared (Jaredite Founder / Brother of the Brother of Jared)

summary.text: Kishkumen was an assassin and a leading member of the Gadianton robbers who carried out two major assassinations. He killed Pahoran, the chief judge of the Nephites, during a public session, though he later escaped. Kishkumen was also chosen to assassinate Helaman, the son of Helaman, who had been elected chief judge. However, a servant of Helaman, who had been given a secret sign by Kishkumen, turned against him and killed him before he could complete the task. The Gadianton robbers fled into the wilderness after Kishkumen's death. Kishkumen's actions were part of a broader conflict involving rival claims to leadership among the Nephites.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Korihor was an anti-Christ who preached heresies of Nehor among the Nephites around 75 B.C. He taught that human success depended on personal strength and shrewdness, denying the coming of the Redeemer and the efficacy of His atonement. He traveled to Zarahemla, Jershon, and Gideon, spreading his doctrines, but was eventually arrested and brought before Alma and Nephihah. Alma declared that God would strike him dumb as a sign, which occurred. Korihor then confessed the power of God and acknowledged being led astray by Satan. Though he begged for mercy, Alma refused to intercede. A proclamation was issued, ending Korihor's influence. Eventually, he became a beggar and was run over and killed in a city of the Zoramites.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Laban was a rich, unscrupulous Israelite in Jerusalem who possessed important records engraved on brass plates that Lehi's family needed for their journey. When Lehi's sons were commanded to retrieve the records, they feared Laban's power and initially refused. After several failed attempts to obtain the records through negotiation, Nephi, guided by the Spirit, slew Laban, who had robbed them and sought their lives. Disguising himself in Laban's armor and using his voice, Nephi tricked Laban's servant Zoram into giving him the plates. This act allowed Lehi's family to obtain the records essential for their spiritual guidance and survival in a new land.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Laman was the eldest son of Lehi and Sariah, born in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah. He was a stubborn and rebellious figure who opposed his father's revelations and proposed the murder of both his brother Nephi and his father. Laman led the Lamanites and was married to one of Ishmael's daughters, from which the royal house of the Lamanites descended. He traveled to Jerusalem twice, once to obtain the plates of brass and again to bring Ishmael and his family. After his father's death, Laman conspired with others to kill Nephi and take control of the colony. His followers became the Lamanites, who later descended into barbarism, living as a cruel, dark-skinned race.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Lemuel was the second son of Lehi and Sariah, born in Jerusalem around 620 or 625 B.C. He was the younger brother of Laman and often followed his brother’s lead, though he lacked Laman’s aggressive hostility. Lemuel supported Laman in all rebellions and conflicts in the Arabian wilderness, including attacks on Nephi. After Lehi’s death, Lemuel and his family joined Laman’s group. He married a daughter of Ishmael, but little is known about his personal life or the time and place of his death. His descendants remained in a secondary position within the Lamanite nation, with no prominent figures emerging from his lineage in either Nephite or Lamanite history.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Limhi was the son of Noah and the third ruler of the colony that left Zarahemla and returned to Lehi-Nephi. His reign was marked by oppression under the Lamanites, who forced his people into bondage and imposed heavy labor. Despite several failed revolts, the Lord fulfilled the prophecies of Abinadi. Limhi led an expedition to find Zarahemla, but the group instead discovered the bones of Jaredites. Later, he communicated with Nephite allies in Zarahemla, and with Ammon and Gideon, he helped his people escape their captors. After reaching Zarahemla, Limhi and his followers were baptized and became members of the church of God.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Mormon was the father of the prophet Mormon and the grandfather of Moroni. He lived in the northern continent until 322 A.C., when he moved his son to the land southward. As a descendant of Nephi, he is noted for instilling in his children a reverence for the Lord and an understanding of the gospel, based on the virtuous character of his son.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Mosiah II was a righteous and beloved king of the Nephites in Zarahemla, ruling from B.C. 125 to B.C. 91. He was consecrated by his father, Benjamin, and led a prosperous and peaceful kingdom. He called Alma, the elder, to lead the church and sent him to teach the people. Mosiah gathered the people to share the experiences of returning refugees and addressed them on important matters. He sent his sons—Ammon, Aaron, Omner, and Himni—to preach to the Lamanites after seeking divine guidance. He also codified the laws of the land, establishing a system of judges. Mosiah translated the Jaredite record from golden plates and gave the sacred plates to Alma. His leadership and spiritual gifts made him highly revered by his people.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nehor was the successful charlatan of the hour, known for his teachings that abolished hell and established a paid order of priests. He expected liberality of support for himself and his assistants, and his doctrine spread widely through the teachings of his followers. Nehor was restive under contradiction, and when Gideon upbraided him for his wicked course, Nehor drew his sword and killed him. Nehor was tried, convicted, and executed on the hill Manti. His doctrine, which allowed people to continue in sin, was later followed by the Amlicites, Amalekites, Amulonites, and Ammonihahites, causing widespread bloodshed and misery.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Omer was a righteous but unfortunate king of the early Jaredites, the son of Shule and father of Jared. Jared rebelled against him, led away half the kingdom, and imprisoned Omer, who fathered Esrom and Coriantumr during his captivity. Esrom and Coriantumr later fought against Jared, defeated his forces, and restored Omer to the throne. Jared then conspired with Akish to assassinate Omer, which partially succeeded, forcing Omer to flee with his family to the North Atlantic coast, passing the hills Shim and Cumorah. He later returned, reigned over the remnants of his people, and anointed his son Emer as his successor. Omer lived to an old age, marked by sorrow and struggle.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Paanchi was a son of Pahoran, the elder, who aspired to the vacant judgment seat after his father's death but was rejected in favor of his brother, Pahoran the younger. He led a revolt supported by many people, was arrested, tried, and condemned to death, which led his followers to hire an assassin named Kishkumen to kill the new Chief Judge. The Gadianton robbers are believed to have originated among the dissatisfied followers of Paanchi.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Lehi-Nephi, Land of was a small region within the land of Nephi, originally settled by the Nephites but later taken over by the Lamanites, who made it the center of their government. It was the valley where the city of Lehi-Nephi stood and is believed to have been located in what is now Ecuador.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Antiparah was a Nephite city located on the southwest border, near the Pacific Ocean, that was captured by the Lamanites during a war led by Amalickiah. The Lamanites stationed a powerful garrison there but later evacuated it to reinforce other Nephite cities they had taken. Antiparah was captured again by the Lamanites during their invasion of the land of Zarahemla.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ishmael, Land of was visited by Ammon, a missionary prince, in 91 B.C. It was ruled by King Lamoni and located down from the land of Nephi (Lehi-Nephi). The land was named after the sons of Ishmael, from whom the ruling dynasty descended. A highway connected Ishmael to Nephi and to the land of Middoni, as evidenced by King Lamoni and his father traveling along it. This suggests the land was situated in the alluvial plains east of the Andes, not in the strip of wilderness between the mountains and the Pacific Ocean.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Zarahemla, City of was the capital of the Nephite nation from about 200 years B.C. to A.C. 30. Situated on the west bank of the Sidon river, it was originally built by the descendants of the people of Mulek and named after their leader, Zarahemla. After the arrival of the Nephites, the two peoples united, and Zarahemla became the seat of government, residence of chief judges and high priests, and the center of civilization. A temple to the God of Israel was built there. The city was captured by the Lamanites multiple times and was destroyed by fire from heaven during the great convulsions of nature that attended the sacrifice of the Lord Jesus. It was later rebuilt, though it is unclear if it regained its status as the chief city.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Antum was a land in North America where a hill called Shim was located, and where Ammaron deposited the sacred records in 321 BC. Mormon later obtained the plates of Nephi from this hiding place and continued the record on them, eventually removing the records to the Hill Cumorah to protect them from the Lamanites. The land of Jashon bordered Antum, and its city was near the site where Ammaron had hidden the records.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Moriancumer, Land of was the place where Jared and his people stayed for four years before crossing the ocean to America. It was named after Mahonri Moriancumer, the brother of Jared, who received revelations from the Lord Jesus there, and where the eight barges that carried them across the ocean were built.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Jerusalem, City of was a Lamanite city within the borders of the land of Nephi.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ripliancum was a large lake, possibly lake Ontario, and part of a chain of lakes. It was the site of a major battle between Jaredite armies led by Coriantumr and Shiz, in which Shiz was defeated and driven toward the hill Ramah, or Cumorah.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Morianton, City of was built by Morianton in the land of the same name. After a dispute with the people of Lehi, the city was captured by Lamanite armies under Amalickiah. By B.C. 63, the Lamanites had fortified the city with a strong garrison and ample supplies. Moroni made preparations to recapture it, but whether he succeeded at that time is unclear. It is likely he did not retake the city until B.C. 61, after dealing with a rebellion at Zarahemla. At that time, Moroni also captured the city of Lehi and other Lamanite-held cities, except for Morianton itself.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nephihah, City of was a significant location in the Book of Mormon, with two possible cities bearing the name. One was located near Manti and the Sidon, while the other was on the Atlantic seaboard, north of Moroni. The latter city was founded by the Nephites in 72 B.C. between Moroni and Aaron, and was later captured by the Lamanites in 67 B.C. Moroni retook it in 61 B.C. through a surprise attack. Elder Orson Pratt noted that the Nephihah mentioned in Alma 56 is distinct from the one referenced in other chapters, highlighting the need for careful distinction between the two locations.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Shazer was a place in the Arabian desert where Lehi and his colony rested while the hunters of the party procured a supply of food.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nephi, Land of was a major region in ancient South America, divided from the land of Zarahemla by a narrow wilderness. The Lamanites occupied the land of Nephi, while the Nephites inhabited Zarahemla. The land of Nephi was rich in resources and covered a large area, with its northern boundary marked by a wilderness stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The Nephites initially settled in the land of Nephi after migrating from Lehi's landing site, but later moved northward to Zarahemla. The land of Nephi was also the home of several cities, which the Lamanites later took over. The region was significant in Nephite history, including the establishment of the Church of Jesus Christ by Alma and the eventual loss of the land to the Lamanites.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Mormon, Waters of was the site where Alma, the elder, baptized Helam and other penitent believers from Lehi-Nephi who accepted the gospel. He buried himself in the water during his first baptism but did not immerse himself again when baptizing others, and he baptized approximately two hundred and four souls there. On the borders of these waters, he organized the Church of Jesus Christ and ordained priests, one for every fifty members.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Moroni, City of was an important Nephite city on the Atlantic coast, built and fortified as an outpost to protect Nephite lands from Lamanite invasion. Named after the Nephite general Moroni, it was captured by Lamanite forces under Amalickiah in B.C. 67 and held until B.C. 61. During this time, Teancum slew Ammoron, the Lamanite king, but was himself killed before returning to his troops. The city was later destroyed at the hour of the Savior's crucifixion, sinking into the depths of the sea and drowning its inhabitants, with its remains now covered by the Atlantic Ocean.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Manti, Land of was situated contiguous to the wilderness at the head waters of the Sidon and lay on the line of march generally taken by the armies of the Lamanites when they invaded Zarahemla. It was the most southerly of all the lands inhabited by the Nephites in the western half of the South American continent after they had moved from the land of Nephi. Its exact boundaries are not defined, and they likely varied considerably at different periods of Nephite history.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Noah, Land of was a region in the land of Zarahemla, contiguous to Ammonihah and situated between the river Sidon and the Pacific Ocean, in the wilderness that bordered that great sea. It was unsuccessfully invaded by the Lamanites in B.C. 81 and B.C. 73, but eventually fell into their control during the time of Moronihah, around B.C. 34, when the Lamanites took control of all of South America.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Desolation, Land of was thickly inhabited by the Jaredites before the time of the Nephites and had Bountiful as its southern border, joining at the Isthmus of Panama. It is believed to have covered the region now known as Central America, with a city of the same name serving as its capital, mentioned only by Mormon in his account of the long series of wars in which he took a prominent part.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Ogath was a place in North America near the hill Ramah (Cumorah), located in the modern State of New York. Shiz gathered people from the Jaredites, including men, women, and children, at Ogath to prepare for a final contest that ultimately led to the destruction of the Jaredite race.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Lemuel, Valley of was a place where Lehi and his colony camped after traveling through the desert near the upper waters of the Red Sea. Lehi named the valley after his son Lemuel and the river running through it after his son Laman, expressing a wish that Lemuel might be as steadfast in keeping the Lord's commandments as the valley itself. After staying in the valley for some time, Lehi continued his journey along the shores of the Red Sea.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Shim, Hill was a location in the land Antum where Ammaron deposited the sacred writings of the Nephites. Ammaron instructed Mormon to retrieve the plates of Nephi from this hill when he turned 24, engraving all the things he observed about the Nephites on them while leaving the remainder of the plates untouched. Later, Mormon removed all the records Ammaron had hidden to a safer place, the Hill Cumorah, as the Lamanites threatened to destroy the land. The hill is also mentioned in the Book of Ether, where it is noted as part of the route of the fugitive king Omer between Moron and Ablom, likely being the same location where the Nephite records were hidden.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Noah, City of was a fortified Nephite city near Ammonihah that played a key role in conflicts with the Lamanites and Amalickiah's forces. After the Lamanites destroyed Ammonihah, they attacked Noah, taking many prisoners, but the captives were later freed by Zoram. Moroni had strongly fortified the city, and when Amalickiah's armies tried to breach it by digging down the walls, they suffered over a thousand dead and wounded, while the Nephites lost only about fifty soldiers.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Manti, City of was the chief city of the land of Manti, situated near the headwaters of the Sidon and recognized as the most southerly city of importance in that region. It suffered greatly from Lamanite invasions and was captured by them during the war led by Amalickiah, becoming an important base for their operations against the Nephites. In B.C. 63, Nephite generals Gid and Teomner recaptured it by stratagem, and Helaman later took his Ammonite and other troops there, making it his headquarters. It was not again captured by the Lamanites during that war, though it likely fell into their hands multiple times in later invasions, as it lay directly in the path of their usual routes into Nephite territory.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Shelem was a mountain named by the Jaredites for its great height, located near the great ocean they were about to cross. The Savior touched the sixteen stones there, which were used to provide light in the barges, and He showed Himself to the brother of Jared, revealing important truths about His coming to the earth in the flesh.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gid (II) was a Nephite city located on the east borders by the seashore, near the cities of Mulek and Bountiful. It became a key location during Amalickiah's raid in 67 B.C., when he captured, garrisoned, and fortified the city, using it as a depot for Nephite prisoners of war. In 63 B.C., Moroni used these prisoners, including women and children, to overthrow the Lamanites and take control of Gid. The Lamanite prisoners were later used to strengthen Gid's fortifications before being moved to Bountiful. Gid was also a site of missionary work by Nephi and Lehi, the sons of Helaman, who traveled there from Bountiful in 31 B.C.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Sebus, Waters of was a watering place in the Land of Ishmael where the king's flocks were watered during the time of Lamoni. It was the site of a conflict between Ammon, the son of Mosiah, and the Lamanite robbers, who sought to scatter the royal cattle.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Lemuel, City of was inhabited by Lamanites who were converted to the Lord by the sons of Mosiah and became part of the people of Anti-Lehi-Nephi. The city's inhabitants later suffered during persecutions against Christian Lamanites, and survivors migrated to the land of Jershon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Moroni, Land of was a district surrounding the city of Moroni, with the Atlantic Ocean as its eastern boundary and the great wilderness separating Nephites from Lamanites along its southern edge. Before being settled by the Nephites around 72 B.C., it was part of that wilderness. The land became central to the final events of a prolonged war initiated by Amalickiah and continued by his brother Ammoron, who was king of the Lamanites. After Ammoron was slain by Teancum in 61 B.C., Moroni drove the Lamanites out of the land, ending the war. This conflict marked a significant turning point in the Nephite-Lamanite struggle.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Shilom, City of was the chief city in the land of Shilom, built by the Nephites before their exodus under Mosiah I. After the Nephites left, the Lamanites occupied it but let it fall into decay. When the Nephites, under Zeniff, regained control of the land, they repaired its dilapidated walls and buildings, and King Noah later enlarged and beautified the city.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Jerusalem, City of (II) was the chief city of the Jews and the home of Lehi, where he prophesied and was led by the Lord. It played a significant role in Nephite chronology, as the year of Lehi's departure from Jerusalem served as their initial date, later expanded with the addition of the 'year of the Judges' in their historical records.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Helam, City of was built by the people of Alma, the elder, in the land of Helam, eight days' journey from the waters of Mormon, after they fled from king Noah's persecutions. The Lamanites later took possession of the city and placed it under the rule of Amulon, who abused the Christian people living there until the Lord enabled their escape. The city was eventually deserted, and its history after that is not recorded.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Judea, City of was a Nephite city located in the southwestern portion of their dominions, between the Pacific Ocean and the land of Manti. It played a key role in military operations from B.C. 66 to 63. Antipus garrisoned the city with about 6,000 men, but they were weakened by the campaign. Helaman arrived with 2,000 young Ammonites, who helped strengthen the city's fortifications. Additional reinforcements later arrived, and after Antipus was slain in a campaign, Helaman took command. Judea remained the Nephites' headquarters for offensive operations until B.C. 63, after which it is no longer mentioned in the Book of Mormon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nehor, Land of was the place to which Corihor fled after rebelling against his father Kib, who ruled in the land of Moron. The land of Nehor is believed to have been near Moron, likely located in or around Central America.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Zarahemla, Land of was a significant region in the Book of Mormon, consisting of two areas: a larger territory spanning much of South America and a smaller district surrounding the capital city of the same name. The land of Zarahemla was central to Nephite life, especially during the reign of King Benjamin and the early days of the Judges. It included cities like Minon, situated above the land of Zarahemla, and was the site of key events, such as Alma taking Amulek from Sidom to the land of Zarahemla. The region also encompassed various cities and lands, including Bountiful, Jershon, and areas along the Atlantic Ocean and Pacific Ocean.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Middoni was a land of the Lamanites where Aaron, Muloki, and Ammah were imprisoned and mistreated. Ammon, guided by divine revelations, decided to rescue his brethren and was joined by Lamoni, the converted king of Ishmael, who believed he could influence Antiomno, the king of Middoni. On their journey, Ammon met Lamoni's father, the ruler of all the Lamanites, traveling from the land of Nephi to Ishmael. Arriving in Middoni, Lamoni gained favor with Antiomno and secured the release of the imprisoned missionaries. Despite their initial cruelty, the Lamanites of Middoni were later converted by the missionaries' teachings.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Cumorah, Hill was a significant location in ancient American history, where the last battles of both the Jaredites and Nephites were fought, leading to the extermination of both peoples. Ammaron hid the holy things in the hill Shim, and later, Mormon removed what had been placed in his care and hid the remaining records in the hill Cumorah. He gave some plates to his son Moroni, who later concealed the treasures in the same hill. The hill is located about three or four miles from Palmyra, New York, and the treasures remained there until the Prophet Joseph Smith exhumed and translated them.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Shemlon, Land of was a region near the city of Lehi-Nephi, contiguous to Lehi-Nephi and likely a neighboring valley. It was part of the Nephite domain until the Lamanites took possession of it after the Nephites' exodus to Zarahemla. The Lamanites retained control of Shemlon and did not cede it to the people of Zeniff, unlike neighboring lands. The land was close enough to Lehi-Nephi that it could be seen from a high tower near the temple. The abduction of Lamanite daughters by the priests of Noah, which occurred in Shemlon, led to a war and had indirect consequences for the Lamanites. Later, during the mission of the four sons of Mosiah, the Lamanites in this land were converted to the Lord.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Jerusalem, Land of was a land of the Lamanites located in the immediate vicinity of the waters of Mormon, probably east or north from Lehi-Nephi. Around 100 B.C., the Lamanites, Amulonites, and various Nephite apostates built a large and thriving city named after their fathers' ancient home in Judea. Aaron, the son of king Mosiah, preached the gospel there, but the city's citizens were too hardened in sin to accept his message. The city was later engulfed in the bowels of the earth during the calamities that followed the crucifixion of the Lord of Life and Glory. Waters rose in its place, and a stagnant sea replaced its grand palaces and synagogues.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Bountiful, City of was the chief city of the Nephites, located near the eastern sea and close to the Isthmus of Panama. It was strongly fortified by Moroni, who used Lamanite prisoners of war to build its walls and enclosure. The city was a key stronghold, preventing Lamanite invasions until the time of Christ. Lamanite prisoners were continuously added to the enclosure as the war turned against them. Nephi and Lehi, sons of Helaman, began their mission at Bountiful. During the crucifixion of Jesus, the city likely suffered less than others, as Jesus appeared to Nephites gathered near the temple there.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Nahom was a place on the journey of Lehi and his company through the Arabian desert where Ishmael died and was buried.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Jershon was a region set apart by the Nephites as the home of the Ammonites, or Christian Lamanites, around 78 B.C. Located north of Zarahemla, it was chosen to protect the Ammonites from the Lamanites. The area was bounded by the Caribbean Sea and the land Bountiful on the north and east, and by Antionum on the south. A church was established there by Ammon, the son of King Mosiah, who served as its high priest. Korihor, an anti-Christ, attempted to undermine the members of Jershon but was escorted out by Ammon. Later, Jershon became a refuge for persecuted gospel believers from Antionum, who were welcomed by the Ammonites. The Nephites eventually occupied Jershon during a war, but no battles were fought there. After this, Jershon is not mentioned again in the Book of Mormon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nephi, City of was frequently referred to as the city of Lehi-Nephi.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gideon, Land of was a valley and city named after the martyr Gideon, who was killed by Nehor with the sword. The valley and its city were closely associated, with the city of Gideon located within the valley. This region played a significant role in several events, including Alma's travels and military actions. Alma traveled to the valley of Gideon, where the Nephites pitched their tents after pursuing the Amlicites. Later, Alma moved his troops toward Zarahemla to protect the capital. Moroni and Pahoran also traveled from Gideon to Zarahemla, following the course of the Sidon river. The valley's location is believed to be east or slightly south of Zarahemla, and it was not known to be part of a larger land area beyond the valley itself.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Nimrod, Valley of was named after Nimrod, a mighty hunter associated with the founding of the Babylonian empire. The Jaredites assembled and organized for their journey in this valley, where the Lord talked with the brother of Jared, though the brother of Jared did not see the Lord, as He was hidden in a cloud.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Sidon, River was the most important river in Nephite history, running through the United States of Colombia and emptying into the Caribbean Sea. It played a crucial role in Nephite civilization, with many of their largest cities built along its banks, including Manti near its headwaters, Gideon, and Zarahemla further north. The river served as a major route to the land of Nephi and was central to numerous battles involving the Lamanites, who invaded along its banks and captured Manti. Key events include the defeat of the Amlicites at hill Amnihu, multiple Lamanite defeats on both sides of the river, and the eventual conversion of the Lamanites, who restored Zarahemla and other lands to the Nephites. The river was also central to the Nephites' movements and the destruction of Zarahemla during the crucifixion of the Redeemer.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Omner, City of was a seaport town on the South Atlantic Ocean or Caribbean Sea, likely named after Omner, the son of Mosiah, who is believed to have founded it. The city was captured by the Lamanites twice, first in B.C. 67 and again around B.C. 35, though the latter event is not explicitly mentioned by name.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ammonihah, City of was a western Nephite city known for the wickedness of its inhabitants, who were mostly followers of Nehor. In B.C. 82, Alma visited the city, but his teachings were rejected. He returned later, was entertained by Amulek, and together they proclaimed the word of the Lord. Their message was scorned, and they were cast into prison, where they were later delivered by the power of God when an earthquake destroyed the prison and killed those inside. The Lamanites destroyed the city by fire the following year, killing all its people. Zeezrom, a lawyer, was a citizen of Ammonihah. After years of desolation, the city was rebuilt and fortified, but the Lamanites retreated when they found Moroni's strong defenses.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Antionum, Land of was a district east of the Sidon inhabited by the Zoramites around 75 B.C. Alma and his followers went there to convince the Zoramites of their errors, but the mission was only partially successful. Those who converted were driven out and found refuge among the Ammonites in Jershon. The unconverted Zoramites joined the Lamanites, who later occupied Antionum with an army. The Nephites countered by placing an army in Jershon. The Lamanites retreated from Antionum into the wilderness, intending to invade Manti, but were thwarted by Moroni and defeated by his troops. Antionum was a large area stretching from the southern wilderness to Jershon on the north, with Zarahemla to the west and the eastern wilderness to the east.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Gideon, Valley of is referenced in connection to the land of Gideon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ani-Anti was a Lamanite village in the land of Nephi where Aaron, Muloki, and Ammah proclaimed the gospel, but the people hardened their hearts. After considerable preaching, the missionaries departed into the land of Middoni.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Ammonihah, Land of was named after a man named Ammonihah and was located near the great western wilderness and the Pacific Ocean. It lay between the river Sidon and the ocean, though its exact location is unknown. The prophet Alma traveled westward to Ammonihah, arriving after a three-day journey from the region of Melek. The land was significant as it was the site of Lamanite military movements, with their armies entering the city from the wilderness side. Its proximity to the wilderness and its position relative to other regions like Melek and Noah influenced the routes and challenges faced by those traveling through the area.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Midian was the son of Abraham and Keturah, and the Midianites were his descendants. They primarily lived in the desert north of the Arabian peninsula. Midian is referenced once in the Book of Mormon, in a quote from Isaiah found in II Nephi, 20:26.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Cumeni was a Nephite city located in the southwest of their possessions, near the Pacific coast. It was initially held by the Lamanites but was captured by the Nephites under Helaman, who laid siege to it, captured its provisions, and forced it to surrender. A failed Lamanite attempt to recapture the city followed, and the Nephite victory was largely due to the bravery of 2,000 young Ammonites led by Helaman.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Lehi, City of was located on the Atlantic seaboard of South America and founded by Lehi, a prominent Nephite general. Its citizens once fled to the camp of Moroni for protection from the city of Morianton, later returning to their homes after the conflict was resolved. The city was captured by Lamanite armies under Amalickiah and remained under their control until the Nephites recaptured it in B.C. 61.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Moron was one of the last and most wicked kings of the Jaredites, ruling alongside his father Ethem in unrighteousness. He faced rebellion from Gadianton-like bands, who wrested half the kingdom from him, but later reconquered his lost provinces. A descendant of the brother of Jared led another revolution, took control of the entire kingdom, and held Moron in captivity for the rest of his life, during which Moron fathered Coriantor, the father of the prophet Ether.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Lehi-Nephi, City of was the capital of the land occupied by the Nephites before their exodus to Zarahemla. The Lamanites took possession of it after the Nephites evacuated, and later ceded it to a Nephite colony under Zeniff, Noah, and Limhi. The Nephites repaired its walls and residences, and during Noah's reign, the city was beautified with a temple and a high tower. Abinadi was martyred there, and Alma established a Christian Church nearby. The city was later evacuated again, becoming the Lamanite capital. Aaron preached to the Lamanites there, and Lehi and Nephi, sons of Helaman, were imprisoned, where God's power was manifested, leading to the conversion of many Lamanites.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Agosh, Plains of was the site of a significant battle during the final war among the Jaredites. Coriantumr and Lib, commanders of opposing armies, fought there after Lib's initial victory in the wilderness of Akish. Coriantumr ultimately defeated Lib, who was slain, and later faced Shiz, Lib's brother, who took command and defeated Coriantumr in another battle at the plains.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Mulek, City of was a Nephite city located on the east coast, near the southern part of South America, about a day's journey south of Bountiful. It was captured by the Lamanites under Amalickiah in 67 B.C., with a Zoramite named Jacob placed in command. Moroni, Lehi, and Teancum later recaptured it in 64 B.C., and Moroni established it as Lehi's headquarters. The city fell again to the Lamanites in 34–33 B.C., but was retaken by Moronihah in 32 B.C. Later, Lehi and Nephi, sons of Helaman, visited the city during a mission to call the people to repentance, traveling from Bountiful to Lehi-Nephi in 30 B.C.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Ephraim, Hill was a location in Central America from which Shule obtained iron ore to make swords and arm his followers in an effort to replace his father Kib on the throne. The hill was situated at no great distance from the land Moron, afterwards Desolation.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Sidom was a place where persecuted members of the true church fled after being driven out of Ammonihah by its citizens. It was apparently located near Ammonihah and is mentioned in the 15th chapter of Alma.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Shilom, Land of was a small district, likely a valley, located near the land of Lehi-Nephi and on the direct route from Zarahemla to Lehi-Nephi. Zeniff and his colony, as well as Ammon and his party, traveled through it. Limhi and his people took a circuitous route around it to avoid detection. A prominent hill north of Shilom was a notable landmark, used by Nephites before they left under Mosiah I. King Noah later built a high tower there. After the Lamanites reoccupied the land, Amulon and his priests became teachers of its people. Eventually, the four sons of king Mosiah converted all the inhabitants of Shilom to the Lord.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Bountiful, Land of was a fertile region in Arabia where Nephi built the ship that carried Lehi's colony to the promised land. It was part of Arabia Felix, known for its abundance and productivity, and located on the shore of the Arabian Sea, which the people called Irreantum. This area should not be confused with another Bountiful in South America, where the Savior appeared to the Nephites.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Lehi, Land of (II) was a small region in South America surrounding the City of Lehi and adjacent to the land of Morianton. A feud erupted in 68 B.C. when the people of Morianton unjustly claimed part of the land of Lehi and sought to assert their claim by force. The people of Lehi fled to the camp of Moroni, the Nephite commander, for protection. Morianton attempted to flee northward but was stopped at the land of Bountiful by Nephite armies. A battle ensued, resulting in Morianton's death. His people were then escorted back to their lands, where they made a peace agreement and united with the people of Lehi, who returned to their homes.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Helam, Land of was located between the cities of Lehi-Nephi and Zarahemla, eight days' journey from the former and fourteen from the latter. It was temporarily occupied by the persecuted people of Alma before falling into the hands of the Lamanites and becoming a subdivision of the land of Nephi.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Riplah, Hill was the site of a major battle between the Nephites and Lamanites in 75 B.C., where both sides suffered heavy losses and the dead were not counted. The Nephites, led by Moroni and Lehi, defeated the Lamanites, who were commanded by Zarahemnah, and the Lamanites surrendered, covenanted to never again wage war against the Nephites, and departed into the wilderness.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Sam was an Israelite of the tribe of Manasseh and the third son of Lehi and Sariah, born and raised in Jerusalem. He accompanied his parents during their exodus from the city around 600 B.C. and traveled with them to the promised land. Though not a leading figure, Sam was obedient and faithful, often following the teachings of his father and the guidance of his brother Nephi. He faced conflict with his elder brothers, who sometimes resorted to violence. After Lehi's death, Sam joined Nephi's group. He married one of the daughters of Ishmael while the group was encamped in the valley of Lemuel.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Samuel, the Lamanite, preached repentance to the citizens of Zarahemla but was cast out by them. A holy angel later visited him, instructing him to return and prophesy to the people. Despite being refused entry, he proclaimed from the city walls about their impending destruction. Many were moved to repent, while others attacked him, but God protected him. He fled to his own country and continued to preach there. His prophecies, including signs at the advent of Jesus, events at His crucifixion, and the eventual destruction of the Nephites, were later quoted by Jesus, Nephi, Mormon, and Moroni. His predictions were fulfilled as recorded in the Book of Mormon.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Sariah was the wife of Lehi and the mother of six sons and some daughters. She lived in Jerusalem before traveling with her family to the promised land. She is mentioned only a few times in the Book of Mormon, but Reynolds suggests she lacked strong faith in Lehi's mission and viewed him as a visionary leading her family into trouble. Four of her sons were adults when they left Jerusalem, while the other two were born during their eight-year journey in the wilderness. Sariah likely gave birth to her daughters in Jerusalem, as she was described as elderly when the family reached the ocean. She endured the hardships of the journey through the Arabian wilderness and likely died before reaching the promised land.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Shiz was a major military commander in the final war between the Jaredite factions, opposing Coriantumr. He was the brother of Lib, whose death at the hands of Coriantumr fueled Shiz's vengeful campaign. Shiz took command of Lib's forces and led a brutal march that devastated the land, destroying cities and killing countless people. He fought Coriantumr in multiple battles, including at the plains of Agosh, the sea shore, the valley of Corihor, the hill Coranor, the great lakes, and the hill Ramah. Despite initial victories, Shiz was ultimately defeated and killed by Coriantumr in the final battle, after both sides had suffered massive losses.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Teancum was a key military leader in the Nephite Commonwealth, commanding the Nephite army of the north and defending the Land Bountiful and the Isthmus of Panama. Moroni dispatched him to stop the migration of the people of Morianton, where Teancum defeated them and slew Morianton. Later, he met and slew the Lamanite leader Amalickiah during a critical battle, preventing the Lamanites from advancing further. Teancum also strengthened the fortifications of the Land Bountiful and the Isthmus. During a later campaign, he advanced near Mulek, and with the help of Lehi, led to the defeat of the Lamanites. In a final act, Teancum slew Ammoron but was slain by the Lamanites before Moroni's forces ultimately defeated them.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
summary.warning: Includes George Reynolds' historical geographic interpretation.

summary.text: Zeezrom was a prominent lawyer in the corrupt city of Ammonihah who led opposition to Alma and Amulek during their ministry. After experiencing the power of God, he repented, was baptized by Alma, and began preaching the message of eternal salvation. He traveled to Sidom, where he was healed by Alma and later accompanied him in ministry, including to the Zoramites. Zeezrom's transformation from a corrupt lawyer to a preacher of righteousness highlights his significant role in the religious revival of the time, and his teachings were referenced by later servants of God.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)

summary.text: Zemnarihah was a chief captain of the Gadianton robbers who led a failed siege against the people of Nephi in A. C. 21. The Nephites, who had stored large amounts of provisions, resisted by constantly harassing the robbers with surprise attacks, causing significant losses. The robbers, weakened by lack of food, attempted to flee north but were blocked by Nephite general Gidgiddoni, who cut off their retreat. After the robbers surrendered, Zemnarihah was executed by being hanged on a tree until dead. Captured robbers were imprisoned, and some who repented were released, while others were punished for their crimes.
summary.attribution: From George Reynolds' Dictionary of the Book of Mormon (1891)
